title: Associated primes in a short exact sequence (any ring)
statement: Let $T$ be a commutative ring. For a commutative ring $T$ and a $T$-module $P$ call a prime ideal $\mathfrak q\subset T$ an *associated prime* of $P$ if $\mathfrak q=\operatorname{Ann}_T(z)=\{a\in T:az=0\}$ for some $z\in P$, and write $\operatorname{Ass}_T(P)$ for the set of them. Let $0\to P'\xrightarrow{f}P\xrightarrow{g}P''\to0$ be a short exact sequence of $T$-modules ($f$ injective, $\ker g=\operatorname{im}f$, $g$ surjective). Then $\operatorname{Ass}_T(P')\subseteq\operatorname{Ass}_T(P)$ (indeed $\operatorname{Ann}_T(f(z'))=\operatorname{Ann}_T(z')$ for $z'\in P'$) and $\operatorname{Ass}_T(P)\subseteq\operatorname{Ass}_T(P')\cup\operatorname{Ass}_T(P'')$. No Noetherian hypothesis is made.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 02M3 (lemma-ass), lines 15130-15150, first two assertions (the third, about direct sums, is not stated here); tag verified in literature/stacks-project/tags/tags: 02M3,algebra-lemma-ass

proof.text: First inclusion. Let $z'\in P'$. Since $f$ is $T$-linear and injective, for $a\in T$ we have $a f(z')=f(az')$, and $f(az')=0$ if and only if $az'=0$. Hence $\operatorname{Ann}_T(f(z'))=\operatorname{Ann}_T(z')$. If $\mathfrak q=\operatorname{Ann}_T(z')$ is prime, then $\mathfrak q=\operatorname{Ann}_T(f(z'))$ with $f(z')\in P$, so $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Ass}_T(P)$. This proves $\operatorname{Ass}_T(P')\subseteq\operatorname{Ass}_T(P)$ and the parenthetical equality of annihilators.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma 02M3 (lemma-ass), proof, first two sentences (lines 15138-15141)

proof.text: Second inclusion, first case. Let $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Ass}_T(P)$, so $\mathfrak q$ is prime and $\mathfrak q=\operatorname{Ann}_T(z)$ for some $z\in P$. Suppose there is $s\in T\setminus\mathfrak q$ with $sz\in\operatorname{im}f=\ker g$, i.e. $g(sz)=s\,g(z)=0$; write $sz=f(z')$ with $z'\in P'$. We claim $\operatorname{Ann}_T(sz)=\mathfrak q$. For $a\in T$: $a(sz)=0\iff (as)z=0\iff as\in\mathfrak q$. If $a\in\mathfrak q$ then $as\in\mathfrak q$ since $\mathfrak q$ is an ideal; conversely if $as\in\mathfrak q$ then $a\in\mathfrak q$ because $\mathfrak q$ is prime and $s\notin\mathfrak q$. So $\operatorname{Ann}_T(sz)=\mathfrak q$. By step 1, $\operatorname{Ann}_T(z')=\operatorname{Ann}_T(f(z'))=\operatorname{Ann}_T(sz)=\mathfrak q$, hence $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Ass}_T(P')$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma 02M3 (lemma-ass), proof, sentences 3-4 (lines 15141-15145): 'If there exists a $g\in R$, $g\notin\mathfrak p$ such that $m'=gm\in M'$ then the annihilator of $m'$ is $\mathfrak p$'

proof.text: Second inclusion, second case. Suppose instead that $sz\notin\ker g$, i.e. $s\,g(z)\neq0$, for every $s\in T\setminus\mathfrak q$. We claim $\operatorname{Ann}_T(g(z))=\mathfrak q$. If $a\in\mathfrak q$ then $az=0$, so $a\,g(z)=g(az)=0$. If $a\,g(z)=0$, then $a\in\mathfrak q$, since otherwise $a$ would be an element of $T\setminus\mathfrak q$ with $a\,g(z)=0$, contrary to the case assumption. Hence $\mathfrak q=\operatorname{Ann}_T(g(z))$ with $g(z)\in P''$, so $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Ass}_T(P'')$. The two cases are exhaustive, which proves $\operatorname{Ass}_T(P)\subseteq\operatorname{Ass}_T(P')\cup\operatorname{Ass}_T(P'')$. (Surjectivity of $g$ is not used; only injectivity of $f$ and $\ker g=\operatorname{im}f$.)

no match (B8): stated for Mathlib's IsAssociatedPrime, which is I prime with I = radical(colon ⊥ {x}) (lines 59-63, 96-98, read with sed -n). Every annihilator-associated prime is radical-associated (a prime equals its radical), but not conversely for non-Noetherian T: in T = k[x_1,x_2,...]/(x_1^2,x_2^2,...), the maximal ideal (x_1,x_2,...) is the radical of Ann(1)=0 but is the annihilator of no element (an element involves finitely many x_i, and x_N for N large does not kill it). So the conclusion of subset_of_injective / subset_union_of_exact for the radical notion does not give the annihilator conclusion, and isAssociatedPrime_iff (line 114) bridges only under IsNoetherianRing: not a one-line specialization; the node is split by its three elementary steps
